title: Static vs Dynamic Typing
summary: Boot.dev instructor explains static versus dynamic typing and argues type inference has removed the old trade-off so static typing is now simply better for large systems.

assertions.quote: the advice has always been static typing is better and the reason being it results in fewer bugs

verdicts.note: Large GitHub studies found a small defect advantage for static typing that weakened on replication, and bug-detectability studies suggest a type checker catches a minority of real bugs, so the benefit is real but modest.

In 729 GitHub projects statically typed languages have a modestly lower association with bug-fix commits than dynamic ones (static functional vs dynamic functional p=0.034), but language explains under 1% of deviance versus project activity, bug fixes are identified by commit-message keywords, and readability is not measured.

The reproduction concludes the GitHub data cannot establish a causal link between language and code quality and even the correlation is questionable; after cleaning, only C++ (more bugs) and Clojure, Haskell, Ruby (fewer) remain significant with exceedingly small effects, a pattern that does not split by static vs dynamic typing.

Static types made undocumented classes faster to use (4 of 5 class-identification tasks) and type errors faster to fix, but gave no benefit on semantic errors; the study measured time, not bug counts, on a 30-class, 1300-line program, so 'fewer bugs' and 'large systems' are untested.

The authors conclude static types act as effective documentation and reduce effort to fix type errors but may not help with semantic errors; the readability mechanism is supported (fewer file switches, less navigation) while defect rates and large codebases were not studied.

Across 80 implementations of one small program, the dynamically typed scripts were not less reliable than the statically typed C/C++/Java programs; C/C++ were the least reliable group and half the Java programs crashed on empty inputs, so no reliability edge for static typing appeared, though only small programs were compared.

assertions.quote: when we don't have to specify types as we're writing our code we're able to write the code a little more quickly
type inference basically gives us the best of both worlds it allows us to have static typing but with a very simple syntax

verdicts.note: Inference clearly cuts annotation burden in Go, Rust and TypeScript, but compile times, generics complexity and type-error comprehension remain costs.

Flow's stronger type inference meant detecting a bug needed fewer annotation tokens (mean 1.7 vs 2.4) and less time (median 133s vs 262s) than TypeScript, so inference does cut annotation burden, but this is per-bug minimal annotation, not whole-program verbosity.

assertions.quote: you can build large production back-end systems in statically typed or dynamically typed languages it's certainly been done both ways
